title: Hippocrates is a research trial which aims to help us understand how the NHS can help people who need a major operation to recover better and more quickly after the operation
official: Health Inequalities in PerioPerative Outcomes – CReATing and Evaluating targeted Support interventions (HIPPOCRATES): a pilot multi-arm randomised controlled trial
summary:
Background and study aim
Every year more than 1.5 million people in the UK have major surgery, and more than 1 in 7 have a serious complication afterwards. People who live in poorer areas are more likely to have complications and to recover less well. This study is testing three types of support, designed together with patients from poorer areas, to find out whether they are practical, acceptable and good value for money. The results will then inform decisions on which intervention(s) should be tested in a larger trial, either alone or in combination with each other.

Who can participate? 
Adults aged 18 or over who are on the waiting list for a major operation (not heart or brain surgery) that usually needs at least 3 nights in hospital, with surgery expected to take place in 1 to 6 months.

What does the study involve? 
Participants are put by chance into one of four groups: 
1. Help to get fitter and healthier before surgery, covering exercise, diet, mental wellbeing and long-term health conditions
2. Financial and welfare support and advice and, if needed, additional support in the form of vouchers
3. A small wearable monitor and text-message check-ins after the operation to spot problems early
4. Usual NHS care

Everyone completes short questionnaires before surgery and at 1, 6 and 12 months afterwards. Some people will be invited to talk about their experience in an interview. Information is available in the five most common languages other than English and in other formats.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
Participants may recover better, but this cannot be guaranteed. The risks are small. Exercise is prescribed by trained staff, and people at higher risk exercise only under supervision. Completing questionnaires takes some time.

Where is the study run from?
The study is coordinated by University College London (UCL), through its Comprehensive Clinical Trials Unit, and will take place at approximately 12 NHS hospitals across England (UK), with the possibility of additional sites.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
Recruitment is expected to run from January 2027 for a minimum of one year. Each participant is followed up for 12 months after their operation. The trial team are seeking additional funding to evaluate new interventions, so it is possible that the duration of this pilot study will be extended. Completion is in October 2029.

Who is funding the study? 
National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Programme Grants for Applied Research (UK).

Who is the main contact? 
HIPPOCRATES trial team, cctu.hippocrates@ucl.ac.uk

interventions.name:
HIPPOCRATES is a pilot platform (multi-arm, multi-stage) trial comparing three co-designed interventions with standard care. Further interventions may be added by protocol modification.

Arm A (intervention 1): Preoperative optimisation and prehabilitation. From randomisation until surgery (1–6 mont

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Age 18 years or older
2. Undergoing elective or expedited major non-cardiac surgery with an expected postoperative hospital length of stay (LOS) of 3 or more days
3. Planned date of surgery between 1 and 6 months from the time of recruitment and randomisation (based on treatment pathway and local waiting times)
4. Able to provide written informed consent
5. Able and willing to complete questionnaires (translated and alternative-format materials available)
Exclusion criteria:
Age under 18 years on the date of recruitment and randomisation
